Date November 2026 · v0.3.1
Product design review · November 2026

Strong identity.
Unfinished system.

Tuner Daemon already looks like a product with a point of view. The gap is between that point of view and the day-to-day experience: two shells, duplicated controls, a mobile layout that does not exist, and a TV screen that can fail silently.

5.2out of 10
Current state: usable on desktop, fragile everywhere else. The visual language is worth keeping. The component system, information architecture and responsive behaviour need a focused six-week overhaul — not a rebrand.
8 screens reviewed 19 findings 4 release-blocking 3 viewports audited
01 · Executive summary

The product has a look. It needs a system.

The review covered every route in the Angular client at 1440 × 900 and 390 × 844, including the guide, modals, theme menus, tables and failure states. The app was built from source and run against the repository's seeded end-to-end fixture, so every screenshot is reproducible.

Tuner Daemon is at its best when it behaves like a control room: dense tables, direct actions, clear status chips, and a dark cinematic palette that makes the live TV screen feel intentional. The reset-data modal is genuinely good — it explains scope, previews exactly what will be removed, and keeps the destructive action visually distinct. Several admin empty states are equally well written.

The problems start where those good pieces meet. Watch and Admin are two separate product shells with separate theme pickers, separate modal conventions, separate spacing and two competing type scales. The mobile experience is a desktop layout cropped to 390 px: the Watch top bar pushes its own settings button off-screen, the guide is wider than the viewport, and the Channels table clips its Match column and every row action. On desktop, icon buttons render as empty boxes because a single global margin rule offsets every icon by 28 px. And when a stream fails, the viewer gets a black rectangle with no message, no timeout and no retry.

23distinct rendered font sizes across eight screens — from a nominal 10-step scale
2theme pickers, modal systems, small-button classes and type-token families
494hard-coded px values in component CSS; 66 inline style attributes in templates
26console errors during the walkthrough; none surfaced in the UI

The one-sentence diagnosis

The interface is inconsistent because it grew screen by screen: each page solved its own problem with its own vocabulary, and the shared layer was added afterwards rather than being the thing everything else was built from.

Five decisions that would change the most

  1. Fix the shell before the surfaces. One header, one theme menu, one modal, one button/table/empty-state vocabulary, used by both Watch and Admin.
  2. Treat mobile as a different layout, not a smaller one. Reflow tables into cards, stack the Watch chrome, and give every control a 44 px target.
  3. Make failure visible. A stream that does not start must show a diagnosis, a retry and a way back to the guide within 15 seconds.
  4. Make status mean one thing. Green for healthy/complete, amber for attention, red for failure, blue for information — never “healthy” in warning amber.
  5. Make the information architecture match the user's questions. Playlist and guide sources belong together; “EPG & Matches” should be named for the job it does; internal keys must never reach the screen.

03 · What is working

Keep the foundation

The overhaul should not sand off the things that already make the product feel authored.

The visual language is distinctive

Cinematic Noir is a real identity: warm amber on near-black, editorial headings, a film-still feel. It carries across dashboard, tables and player. Nine themes exist, and the infrastructure for them is sound.

Shared primitives already exist

.stat, .btn, .glass-card, .state, a single spinner, a global :focus-visible ring and a reduced-motion rule. The problem is adoption, not invention.

Some states are exemplary

The reset modal previews the exact rows and bytes it will delete. Sources and Dashboard have actionable empty states. Diagnostics has a real retry path when loading fails.

  • Distinct, coherent cinematic identity
  • Self-hosted fonts; no external dependency
  • Global focus ring and reduced-motion support
  • Dense, readable desktop tables
  • Reproducible e2e fixture and visual baseline
  • Consequence-first destructive flow
04 · Findings

Nineteen findings, ranked by cost to the user

P0 blocks a core task or loses trust. P1 makes the product slower to learn or inconsistent. P2 is polish that compounds. Each finding includes the evidence and the smallest fix worth shipping.

P0

Watch is unusable on a phone

Responsive

At 390 × 844, the Watch layout is still a desktop canvas. The top bar overflows: the Admin/Settings button sits at CSS x = 395–439, entirely off-screen. The channel info bar sits entirely inside the lower-third overlay’s 240 px region (189 px overlap), clipping the programme title, time and the guide/star controls. The wordmark wraps to two lines. Opening the guide makes it worse: the panel is wider than the viewport, so “PROGRAM GUIDE”, the category filters and the right-hand guide columns are cut off with no horizontal scroll.

FixMobile Watch needs its own composition: a single compact header (brand, guide, overflow menu), a stacked info card rather than two overlays, and a guide that becomes a horizontally paged channel list or a vertical “now/next” list. Add a 44 px minimum target and safe-area padding. Validate at 320, 390 and 768 px.
P0

Admin tables do not adapt to mobile

Responsive

The Channels page keeps six desktop columns at 390 px. The Match column and every row action are clipped at the right edge; the only hint is a half-cut “M” in the header. Sources has an explicit 820 px minimum table width (sources.component.css:19), so it has the same problem. There is no card view, no priority-column strategy and no visible scroll affordance. The filter card above the table consumes nearly half the first screen before a single channel is visible.

FixBelow 768 px, render list rows as cards: logo, name, number, now-playing and match status in a two-column grid, with a single “Edit” action. Collapse filters into a “Filters” disclosure with a result count. Keep the desktop table unchanged above the breakpoint.
P0

A failed stream is indistinguishable from a black screen

Trust

Six seconds after load, the video element reports readyState 0, networkState 2, loading false, and no error overlay. The console records the failures; the viewer sees a black rectangle and a lower third that says a programme is playing. The template does contain a “Stay Tuned” overlay for error, but none of the playback paths raise it for a stream that never starts, and there is no start-up timeout. The user cannot tell whether the app is loading, broken or tuned to a dead channel.

FixAdd a start-up watchdog (8–12 s) and a “stream unavailable” state with the failure reason, Retry, previous/next channel, and Open diagnostics. Treat HLS and native video paths identically. Make this a release gate: no black screen can persist for more than 15 s.
P0

Icon buttons render as empty boxes

Craft

Every .icon-btn on Watch is a 44 × 44 button, but its 18 × 18 icon is offset by +28 px right and +28 px down — pinned to the bottom-right corner. The cause is one global rule: .icon-btn svg { margin: 1em; width: 18px; height: 18px; } (styles.css:1186). At normal viewing distance the DVR, server, theme and admin controls read as four empty rectangles. The same rule affects the guide and favourite controls in the channel bar.

FixRemove the margin and set icon size explicitly (18/20/24 px tokens). Add a component test that asserts the icon box is centred within the button, and include the Watch chrome in visual regression.
P1

Two shells, two theme pickers, two vocabularies

Consistency

Admin offers “Choose Theme” from a dropdown in the sidebar; Watch offers “Select Theme” from a dropdown in the top bar. They share the same nine themes but not the same markup, row shape, selected state or copy. The Admin version is also clipped by the viewport: the menu starts near the bottom of the sidebar and runs past the edge, with no scroll. Nothing about the two experiences says “same product” beyond the palette.

FixExtract one ThemeMenu component (button, panel, options, selected state, keyboard support, scrolling). Use it in both shells. Reduce the default list to four curated themes with an “All themes” disclosure, and add a light/high-contrast option rather than a tenth dark variant.
P1

Modal behaviour depends on which page you are on

Consistency

Admin dialogs use appModalFocus, [role="dialog"] semantics and a dismiss handler. Watch's “Schedule Local Recording” modal has none of that: no focus trap, no dialog role, no Escape contract, and a different close control (&times; instead of the lucide X). Only the Watch “Server Connection” modal uses the shared directive. The result is that keyboard and screen-reader users get a usable dialog in Admin and a focus escape in Watch.

FixOne <app-modal> with title id, focus trap, initial focus, Escape, backdrop click, scroll lock and a single close icon. Migrate all nine call sites; delete the per-page markup.
P1

The design system is duplicated, then bypassed

System

There are two type-token families in the same :root (--text-* and --font-*), 23 distinct rendered font sizes, 494 hard-coded px values in component CSS, 66 inline style attributes, 17 unique hex colours in component CSS, and 26 radius declarations that mostly bypass the radius tokens. Both .small-btn and .btn-sm exist. The login overlay references --bg-dark, which is not defined anywhere. The system is present enough to be ignored, which is worse than none.

  • Type: 10.08, 10.4, 11, 11.2, 11.52, 11.68, 12, 12.48, 12.8, 13, 13.12, 13.33, 13.6, 14, 14.4, 15.2, 16, 18, 22, 24, 28, 28.8, 36 px.
  • Components: four close-button treatments (close-modal-btn, close-btn, diag-close-btn, text &times;), two small-button classes, two theme menus, two shells.
FixDeclare one scale and enforce it. Delete the legacy family, replace raw px with tokens in the touched components, ban inline layout styles in review, and add a stylelint rule for hex literals outside the token file. Target ≥95% token coverage in the eight screens.
P1

Status colours contradict their labels

Semantics

On the Dashboard, the word “healthy” is rendered in the warning colour. On DVR, “Completed” is amber badge-warning, “Missed” is blue badge-info, and “Scheduled” is also amber. The semantics are inverted: success reads as attention, failure reads as information. On Sources, three stat cards are filters (they are buttons with pressed state) and “Failing” is a plain div — the one card a user would most want to click is the only one that does nothing.

FixDefine five semantic tones and a status map: success healthy/completed/recording, warning attention/degraded, danger failed/missed/error, info scheduled/cancelled. Make every stat that represents a filter a button; give non-interactive stats a visibly different treatment.
P1

Lists do not answer the question the page asks

Content

Channels is the page where a user asks “what is on right now?” — and every row says “No Info” while the Dashboard reports 96 guide programmes. The EPG & Matches table has a column titled “Match Type / Confidence Score” that shows only an “Exact” tag and never a score. The Dashboard's scheduled-jobs row renders as “Daily EPG UpdateEvery 12 hours” because .stat-row is used in the template but never defined in CSS. The sync-progress disclosure uses a literal ▶ character rather than the icon system.

FixDecide the primary question for each page and make the first column answer it. For Channels, show current programme title, time remaining and a progress indicator; fall back to “No guide data” with a link to matching. Remove “score” from the EPG header until a score exists. Fix the schedule row with a real flex/grid rule and space between label and value.
P1

Information architecture splits one job across three pages

IA

Adding a playlist lives in Settings (“Playlist configuration”), but sources are managed in Sources; guide reliability lives as a tab inside “EPG & Matches”, not with the guide sources; DVR's “My Recordings” means browser-local recordings, while “Server Recordings” is the actual DVR. The nav says “EPG & Matches” while the route is /diagnostics and the page is about match quality. A new user has to learn the internal pipeline before they can configure it.

FixGroup by the user's job: Sources owns playlists, guide feeds, source health and reliability. Guide owns match quality and channel mapping. Settings owns automation, output and metadata. Recordings separates server and browser storage with plain labels (“On this device”). Add a first-run path: Sources → Sync → Watch.
P1

Internal vocabulary leaks into the interface

Language

The Settings page shows an active playlist as a chip labelled playlist with a custom tag — a generic auto-label, not the name of anything the user chose. The same page asks users to “Sync iptv-org Repo”, offers “FAST channel presets”, and explains “Metadata enrichment”. Diagnostics asks about “Grab-capable match sources”. DVR mixes “DVR”, “Server Recordings”, “My Recordings”, “Local” and “System”. Capitalisation wobbles between Title Case, sentence case and ALL CAPS within one screen (“ACTIONS”, “Scheduled Jobs”, “SHOW SYNC PROGRESS & LOGS”).

FixWrite a 40-term glossary and enforce it in copy review. Render each playlist’s real name and host, not an auto-label plus “custom”. Replace “repo” with “catalogue”, “grab” with “fetch guide data”, “enrichment” with “add artwork and descriptions”, “FAST” with “free channels”. Use sentence case for labels and headings, and reserve uppercase for table headers and eyebrows only.
P1

Failed logos are rendered as broken-image glyphs

Resilience

The fixture deliberately points channel logos at an unreachable host, which is a realistic CDN failure. The UI shows the browser's broken-image glyph plus the alt text “Logo” in Watch, and broken thumbnails in Channels, Diagnostics and DVR. There is no monogram fallback, no retry/backoff and no visual difference between “no logo” and “failed to load”.

FixOne <app-channel-logo> with initials/colour fallback, onerror suppression, lazy loading and a request budget. Use it everywhere a channel or recording thumbnail appears.
P2

Grids leave orphan cards

Layout

Dashboard has four actions in a three-column grid, so “Reset data” sits alone on a second row. DVR has four cards in a three-column grid, same problem. Settings has six FAST presets in a five-column grid. The layout looks unfinished at common desktop widths, and the orphaned destructive action gets more visual weight than it deserves.

FixUse repeat(auto-fit, minmax(240px, 1fr)) with a max column count, or intentionally make the last row span. Keep destructive actions out of the primary action grid.
P2

Watch renders the same information twice

Layout

With the guide open, the lower-third overlay shows channel number, name, category and programme over the video; the channel-info bar immediately below repeats the same fields and adds a second set of guide/favourite/layout controls. The duplication costs vertical space and splits the controls across two regions with no rule about which one is authoritative.

FixChoose one: keep the lower third only while the video is the focus, and collapse to the info bar when the guide is open. Move guide/favourite controls into one action cluster in the info bar.
P2

Accessibility gaps are structural, not cosmetic

A11y

The global focus ring and reduced-motion rule are genuinely good. Beneath them: Watch has no h1 or heading structure at all; the volume button, guide navigation buttons and the mobile hamburger have no accessible name; the volume range input has no label; 28 controls on the open guide are below 32 × 32; the settings number input is unlabelled; and the guide uses 10–11.5 px text. --text-muted on a glass card measures 4.37:1, under the 4.5:1 AA threshold for normal text. The mobile Watch admin link is off-screen, so a sighted keyboard user only discovers it when focus lands there.

FixAdd accessible names to every icon-only control; give Watch a visually-hidden h1 and landmark regions; label every input; raise the minimum type size to 12 px for micro copy and 13 px for secondary; increase tap targets to 44 px; verify contrast per theme with an automated test. Add axe-core to the Playwright suite with a zero-serious-violations gate.
P2

Three icon languages in one product

Craft

Lucide icons coexist with text glyphs (▶ ▼ ✓ × ★ ☆ → ⤢) and emoji (📡 STANDBY, 📺 STAY TUNED). Some controls use the lucide component, others a text character sized by font. The visual weight, baseline and stroke width change from screen to screen; the star is the only visible control in the Watch deck.

FixLucide only, 1.75 px stroke, three sizes (16/20/24). Replace the star with star/star-filled, the disclosure triangles with chevron-down, and the emoji with icons plus text. Add a lint rule for emoji/glyph buttons.
P2

Settings is a long page with no map

Efficiency

Playlist, presets, custom URL, IPTV-org, EPG duration, language, output paths, metadata, retention and save all live in one scroll. There is no section nav, no sticky action bar, and the save button is far from the fields it commits. On mobile, the six preset cards become six full-width blocks before the custom URL appears.

FixAdd a section rail (Playlist, Guide, Output, Metadata, Recording) and a sticky save bar that shows dirty state. Collapse presets into a two-column compact grid or a select. Group related fields into cards with one primary action each.
P2

Loading and confirmation feedback is inconsistent

Feedback

All data screens use a centred spinner rather than skeletons, so the page height jumps when content arrives. Source removal and channel-match clearing rely on different confirmation patterns; some destructive actions are one click. The shared confirm service has thoughtful copy, but async buttons do not consistently show a pending state, and the Watch schedule dialog bypasses the shared modal shell.

FixAdopt skeleton rows for tables and card grids, and a button-level pending state for every async action. Keep the existing confirm service and toasts; they are already the right pattern.
P2

All nine themes are dark, and the menu is clipped

Accessibility

The theme system is a strength, but every option is a dark palette; there is no light or high-contrast mode for daylight or low-vision use. The Admin menu opens near the viewport bottom and clips its last rows without a scroll container. Theme names (“Tuner Daemon (Cyber Lime)”, “Omni Station”, “Aether Vision”) describe moods, not the differences a user is choosing between.

FixShip four themes: Noir (default), Daylight (light, AA), High contrast and Neon (accent variant). Give each a one-line description and a swatch preview. Make the menu scrollable with a max-height and a search/“reduce motion” note.
05 · Screen review

Screen by screen

What each screen is for, what to keep, and the single change that would most improve it. Screenshots use the seeded fixture; unreachable media hosts are intentional.

06 · Improvement plan

A six-week cycle, in four gates

The sequence is deliberate: stop the trust-breaking failures first, then remove duplication, then change the mental model, then polish. Each cycle ends with a measurable gate. Estimates assume one front-end engineer plus a half-time designer, with QA in the loop.

Order of operations

Stabilise (P0, week 1–2) → Unify (P1 system, week 2–4) → Clarify (IA and language, week 4–5) → Polish & measure (P2, week 5–6). Do not start with a new visual theme; the current one is not the problem.

Cycle 0 — Baseline & guardrails

Week 0 · 2 days
Make the problems measurable so the overhaul cannot quietly regress.
  • Add a Playwright screenshot matrix at 320, 390, 768, 1024 and 1440 px for all eight screens, plus guide, dialogs, empty and error states.
  • Add axe-core and custom assertions: no horizontal overflow, no interactive element outside the viewport, no tap target under 44 px, no accessible-name gaps, no console errors.
  • Inventory components and tokens; publish the “one of each” list and freeze new one-off variants.
  • Add a performance/UX budget: CSS LOC, token coverage, number of distinct font sizes.
Gate 0The matrix runs in CI on every PR; the baseline report reproduces the 19 findings; the team agrees on the target component list.

Cycle 1 — Stabilise

Week 1–2 · 8–10 days
Remove the failures that make the product feel broken.
  • Watch: reflow header, lower third and guide for mobile; 44 px targets; safe areas; no off-screen controls.
  • Admin: responsive card rows for Channels, Sources and DVR below 768 px; collapsible filters; sticky primary action.
  • Playback: start-up watchdog, visible error state, retry, next/previous channel, diagnostics link; unify HLS/native paths.
  • Craft sweeps: fix .icon-btn centring; <app-channel-logo> fallback; status tone map; remove the orphan action card.
Gate 1Zero off-screen controls and zero horizontal overflow from 320–1440 px. Failed streams surface an actionable state within 15 s. All icons centred. No broken-image glyphs in any screenshot.

Cycle 2 — Unify

Week 2–4 · 8–10 days
One system, two contexts: the same components in Watch and Admin.
  • Build and migrate the core kit: Button, IconButton, Modal, ThemeMenu, Stat, StatusBadge, Table/DataList, EmptyState, SectionHeader, Toast.
  • Collapse the two type families into one scale; delete raw hex/px in the eight screens; remove .btn-sm/.small-btn duplication; define --bg-dark or remove it.
  • One modal with focus trap and one close icon; migrate every call site.
  • One theme menu; four curated themes including light and high-contrast; fix scrolling and clipping.
Gate 2Component inventory has one implementation per pattern. Token coverage ≥95%. CSS LOC down ≥20%. Zero duplicate modal/theme/button variants. Visual diffs reviewed and approved.

Cycle 3 — Clarify

Week 4–5 · 6–8 days
Make the product explain itself without a manual.
  • New IA: Sources owns playlists/feeds/health; Guide owns matching; Recordings owns server and device; Settings owns automation/output/metadata.
  • Rename “EPG & Matches” to “Guide & matching”; split “My Recordings” into “On this device”; move reliability out of the match table.
  • First-run path and checklist: add a source → run a sync → watch; surface it on Dashboard and in empty states.
  • Copy pass: 40-term glossary, sentence case, no internal keys, plain-language help, shortcut sheet (“G”, arrows, Esc).
Gate 3Five first-time users complete “add a playlist”, “find why a channel has no guide” and “record a programme” with ≥80% success and no moderator help. Zero internal identifiers on screen. Every nav label is understood by 5/5.

Cycle 4 — Polish & measure

Week 5–6 · 4–6 days
Lift the floor on accessibility and perceived quality, then measure.
  • Minimum 12 px micro / 13 px secondary type; 44 px targets; per-theme contrast verification; visible focus in Watch; hidden h1/landmarks.
  • Skeletons for tables and cards; shared confirmations; pending states on async buttons.
  • Lucide-only icon sweep; remove emoji and glyph buttons; consistent disclosure chevrons.
  • Motion pass: 150–250 ms, reduced-motion parity, no hover lift on non-interactive cards.
Gate 4axe-core serious violations 0. SUS ≥75 with five users. Time-to-first-sync under 3 minutes on a clean install. Lighthouse accessibility ≥95. No P0/P1 finding left open.

What not to do

  • Do not start with a rebrand. The palette and type pairing are the strongest part of the product; changing them would hide the structural problems for a release.
  • Do not add more themes. Nine dark variants increase test surface without improving comprehension. Consolidate first, then add a light/high-contrast pair.
  • Do not make Watch and Admin identical. They should share components and language, not density. Watch remains immersive; Admin remains dense.
  • Do not ship a mobile “scale down”. Tables and the guide need different compositions, not smaller type.
07 · Design direction

Six principles for the rebuild

These are the decisions to use when a new screen does not have an obvious precedent.

01

One system, two contexts

Watch and Admin share tokens, components and vocabulary. Context changes density and chrome, not the rules.

02

Each screen answers one question

Channels: what is on now? Sources: is my data arriving? DVR: did it record? Lead with that answer and one primary action.

03

Status is a promise

One colour, one meaning, every time. Green means healthy or complete. Amber means attention. Red means failure. Blue never means failure.

04

Desktop density, mobile clarity

Keep the table density on large screens. On phones, reflow to cards and disclosure — never shrink a six-column table.

05

Every failure is visible and recoverable

No silent black screens, broken images without fallbacks, or failed requests without a next step.

06

TV first, not TV only

Design for the remote and the keyboard: focus order, 44 px targets, a visible focus ring in player chrome, and a shortcut sheet.

09 · Method & evidence

How this review was produced

No opinions without a reproduction. The app was built from source and run against the repository's seeded end-to-end fixture at .e2e-fixture. Screenshots were captured with Playwright/Chrome at 1440 × 900 and 390 × 844 (2× DPR), with a 1920 × 1080 pass for the wide guide.

Environment

  • Angular 21.2 client, v0.3.1, production SSR build
  • API on :45210, web on :45211, fixture DB
  • Chrome stable, headless, DPR 1 and 2
  • Viewports: 390 × 844, 1440 × 900, 1920 × 1080
  • Data: 12 channels, 96 programmes, 3 sources, 4 recordings

Caveat

The fixture deliberately points channel logos and streams at fixture.invalid. That is useful: it exposes how the UI behaves when remote media is slow or dead. It is not evidence that production logos are broken — it is evidence that there is no fallback when they are.

Automated checks used

  • Off-screen element and document-overflow audit
  • Accessible-name audit for buttons, inputs and links
  • Tap-target measurement (width/height < 32/44)
  • Computed font-size census
  • Video element state after 6 s
  • Icon bounding-box geometry
  • WCAG contrast calculation for token pairs

Scoring rubric

9–10: excellent, no material issue. 7–8: strong, minor friction. 5–6: usable but inconsistent or slow to learn. 3–4: a core task is impaired. 1–2: unusable. The overall score is a weighted mean; weights favour the daily admin loop and accessibility because this is an operational tool.

Bottom line

Tuner Daemon does not need a new identity. It needs the identity it already has to be enforced by a system: one shell, one vocabulary, one responsive strategy, one visible failure path. The four release-blocking issues are small in code and large in trust — and they can all be closed in the first cycle.
